rejected_exemplar.subject_line: The June 1 frailty rule moved the exemption math you were planning around
rejected_exemplar.eyebrow_line: A public read on where the 43 states actually stand after CMS changed the definition
rejected_exemplar.message_body:
CMS issued an interim final rule on June 1, 2026 that narrowed what counts as medical frailty. If the exemption approach your team built predates it, the ground under that plan moved, and the public KFF Work Requirements Tracker already shows how little slack is left before the January 1, 2027 deadline that all 43 affected states share.

The tracker also shows the states are not moving together. Nebraska began enforcing federal work requirements early under a May 1, 2026 state plan amendment, while other states still show no declared implementation path. Read next to the June 1 rule, that spread is the story: the states that locked their exemption assumptions before the rule now carry the most rework, and the outreach window between June 30 and August 31, 2026 is already open, so the time to rebuild is not sitting in the future.

The cost of the build is public too. Iowa's system-change filing puts its work at a minimum of $20 million, and Wisconsin's runs near $6 million for a pair of changes. Most agencies will route that through the IT vendor they already hold. The part the vendor does not touch is the part that just changed: reconciling the new frailty definition with exemption logic, outreach, and eligibility rules before the clock runs out.

That reconciliation is a policy judgment made under a deadline, and HMA's consultants have made it from the inside. They came out of state Medicaid director and senior policy roles, so the read on what the June 1 rule actually shifts, and what a defensible exemption posture looks like now, comes from people who have answered for that call in the chair you are sitting in.

State budget and system-change filings (Wisconsin, Iowa)
